evidence.title: Cognitive forcing reduces acceptance of incorrect recommendations in one task
evidence.observation: Authors report that cognitive-forcing designs reduced acceptance of incorrect recommendations compared with simple explainable-AI interfaces in an experiment with 199 participants performing meal-substitution decisions with simulated AI.
evidence.evidence_standing: Bounded observation (researcher-reported experiment; not independently reproduced)
evidence.glossary_fit: Illustrative, bounded; does not establish generality

source_locations.SRC-016: Sections 3.1–3.5 (task, conditions, simulated AI, participants), 4.1 (incorrect predictions), 5 (cognitive motivation), 6 (discussion)

evidence.limitations: Designs producing stronger correction received worse subjective ratings; benefits varied with motivation for effortful thinking. Controlled nutrition task does not establish durable compliance, high-stakes effectiveness, or performance under shrinking deadlines. EVID-019 shows that explanations can improve error rejection without forcing in another task; these are different tasks, not failed replications.
evidence.open_questions: Transfer to operational oversight and effective intervention remains unestablished.
evidence.support_assessment: Attributed research finding; not independently reproduced by the Commons.
evidence.dispute_status: No explicit correction located in bounded search; not a systematic retraction clearance
evidence.verification_status: Not independently verified by the Commons

terms.name: Meaningful human control
terms.definition: A condition in which people retain adequate information, independent judgment, authority, and practical means to redirect consequential activity. A nominal human-in-the-loop approval does not, by itself, demonstrate this capacity.

relationships.explanation: Task-level assessment and correction do not establish full operational authority, independence, or effective intervention.
